Article Title: Italian jobs, French connections and Berlin walls: Chess’s European tour
Article Text:
Aarav Dengla is India's 93rd Grandmaster (GM)

The Italian Job

The Sicilian Defence

El Matador

The Spanish Opening, also known as the Ruy Lopez, is a classic chess opening that starts with the moves 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5.

The French Connection

Position after 1.e4 e6

Berlin Wall

The starting position of the Berlin Defense is reached after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6

For a centuries-old game that has witnessed and survived the rise and fall of empires, kings and kingmakers, chess has developed a vocabulary of its own. This vocabulary is a veritable tour of the people and places that have had major influence on the game.To an ordinary person, 1.e4 c5 is simply a sequence of moves; to a chess player it is the Sicilian Defence. Why Sicily and not Shanghai or St. Louis? Or why Ruy Lopez and not Roy Lampert?I have long been curious to learn the history behind people and places after whom various chess openings and variations are named. One column won’t be enough to cover these places and people; one would have to write an entire book.Europe dominates these places in chess vocabulary. There are historical reasons behind the European dominance, but that is material for another column. In this column, I will write about a few well-known places that many readers may themselves have visited.Sicily is well known for Mount Etna, historical ruins and lovely beaches. It is also associated with an often-played move in chess. After 1.e4, Black answers 1...c5, refusing to mirror White in the center and instead attacking it from the side.The Sicilian Defence is played from club level to world championship matches.Its ancestry dates back at least to the Italian theoretician Giulio Cesare Polerio. In a manuscript dating from around 1594, Polerio analysed the sequence 1.e4 c5, making his work one of the earliest known discussions of the opening.Polerio did not name the opening. In 1813, the English writer Jacob Henry Sarratt cited an older Italian source that called it il gioco siciliano (the Sicilian game), helping to establish the term in chess literature.The opening’s reputation was uneven. Some influential theorists dismissed it as an irregular response to 1.e4, while strong nineteenth-century players showed its counterattacking promise.Over time, its eccentricity became its chief appeal: Black does more than defend the center;Black creates imbalance from the first move. The Sicilian Defence is an aggressive counterpunch. It may not always succeed, but then again, neither do all Italian jobs!Watching a matador face a raging bull in the rings of Las Ventas in Madrid is an experience you remember for life. Twelve hundred pounds of hulk, armed with two sharp horns, charging at a matador with a singular objective of goring him. The matador deftly moves aside at the last moment with a calm precision.I like to think of Spanish Opening as El Matador for the serenity with which White opens and builds the game against Black.Better known as the Ruy Lopez, the Spanish Opening is one of the foundations of classical opening theory. Its most famous early treatment appeared in Libro de la invencion liberal y arte del juego del axedrez, published at Alcalá de Henares in 1561 by the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura.López did not invent 3.Bb5; the idea appears in earlier sources, including the Göttingen manuscript from around the late fifteenth century. His contribution was to give the move one of its first systematic analyses. His work proved so influential that the opening came to bear both his name and, across much of Europe, his nationality: the Ruy Lopez, or Spanish Opening.My chess journey is intricately linked to France. I have fond memories of that country. I made my first IM norm in Paris and have generally done well in tournaments in France.Named after this wonderful country, the French Defence owes its identity to a correspondence match between Paris and London in 1834, in which members of the Paris team adopted this defensive technique.French Defence looks modest. Black does not immediately challenge White’s pawn on e4. Instead, Black prepares ...d5 by playing 1…e6 and builds a compact central structure. Yet the opening creates exactly the sort of strategic tension that has kept it alive for nearly two centuries.For almost three decades, the Berlin Wall stood as a symbol of the ideological and geopolitical battles between the two world superpowers. When the wall came down in 1989, the pieces on the geopolitical chessboard were rearranged, followed by the reunification of modern-day Germany.Berlin Defence, also nicknamed Berlin Wall, is one of the old branches of the Spanish Opening. It gets its name from the Berliners who analysed its variations deeply. It is a very defensive opening by Black. So solid that White must work hard to break it down (hence the nickname Berlin Wall).The opening appears in the 1843 edition of Handbuch des Schachspiels edited by Paul Rudolf von Bilguer. It was deployed in the world championship contests in the late 19th century.It went out of fashion for almost a century until Vladimir Kramnik revived it in the 2000 World Championship match against Garry Kasparov. Kramnik played it in four games (all with Black) and frustrated Kasparov with draws in all four games. After losing the championship to Kramnik, Kasparov attributed his loss to Kramnik’s superior preparation with Black. The four openings above are among the best-known of those named after equally well-known Places.Read also: Before AI, there was the Mechanical Turk: The chess machine that wasn’t (Aarav Dengla is India’s 93rd Grandmaster. He is a keen observer and student of world history in general and chess history in particular.)
Article Summary: The Sicilian Defence is played from club level to world championship matches. After 1.e4, Black answers 1...c5, refusing to mirror White in the center and instead attacking it from the side. The French Defence owes its identity to a correspondence between Paris and London in 1834.

Article Title: Manchester City make shock move to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool in £85m deal: Reports
Article Text:
Manchester City have opened talks for Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, with reports valuing the Dutchman at £85m/ Image: X

Why could Gakpo leave Liverpool?

Gakpo has been an important part of Liverpool's attack

City preparing for a busy finish to the window

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manchester City have opened talks with Liverpool over a potential move for Cody Gakpo, with the Dutch forward emerging as one of the biggest names who could still change clubs before the transfer window closes.According to reports, City made formal contact with Liverpool on Saturday evening regarding a move for the 27-year-old. ESPN, citing its own sources, reported that discussions between the clubs had gathered pace and that Liverpool value Gakpo at £85 million ($115m).Gakpo has also attracted interest from Tottenham Hotspur, but sources cited by BBC Sport indicate that Manchester City is the forward's preferred destination should he leave Anfield.The possibility of Gakpo's departure comes at a particularly interesting point in Liverpool's transfer window. The Reds have agreed a deal to sign Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola for a fee that could rise to £123 million, according to BBC Sport, and Liverpool are understood to want another forward through the door before allowing Gakpo to leave.Liverpool have an interest in Brighton winger Yankuba Minteh and Crystal Palace forward Ismaïla Sarr, with the club having already seen bids for both players rejected, according to reports.That means Gakpo's situation is not simply a matter of whether City are prepared to meet Liverpool's valuation; the Reds also need to make sure they have sufficient attacking options before sanctioning his exit.ESPN reported that City have been encouraged by Gakpo's interest in a move to the Etihad Stadium and are pressing ahead with negotiations.Gakpo joined Liverpool from his boyhood club PSV Eindhoven in January 2023 and has since scored 33 goals in 91 Premier League appearances.The forward has also started the new season in good form. He scored in Liverpool's opening league fixture, a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United, and then provided the assist for Alexander Isak's goal in Saturday's 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest at Anfield.Gakpo started against Forest despite the growing speculation surrounding his future, with Liverpool twice having to come from behind to rescue a point.His possible departure would therefore leave Andoni Iraola with another significant attacking decision to make, particularly with Liverpool already close to bringing Barcola into the squad.Manchester City are also expected to remain active during the final days of the transfer window.According to ESPN, City have already agreed a deal with Palmeiras for Brazilian winger Allan, while Savio and Omar Marmoush have both left the club to join Tottenham this summer.The club have also been working on their midfield, having already spent more than £200 million on that area following the departures of Bernardo Silva and Rodri, with Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi among their additions.ESPN's sources say City are expected to make at least one late bid for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernández as well as continuing discussions over Gakpo.For Liverpool, meanwhile, the decision is becoming increasingly time-sensitive, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday, September 1. The club must now weigh City's interest against its own need to maintain numbers in attack, particularly with Barcola's arrival close and further moves for Minteh or Sarr still being pursued.
Article Summary: Manchester City have opened talks with Liverpool over a potential move for Cody Gakpo. The Dutch forward could still change clubs before the transfer window closes. Liverpool have agreed a deal to sign Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola for a fee of £123 million.

Article Title: Michael Carrick says it is ‘lazy’ to claim Man Utd lacked passion after embarrassing 2-0 defeat to newly promoted Hull City
Article Text:
Manchester United's interim head coach Michael Carrick walks on the pitch at the end of the English Premier League soccer match between Manchester United and Nottingham Forest in Manchester, England, Sunday, May 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Dave Thompson)

Carrick rejects claims United lacked desire

Carrick wants United to respond

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Michael Carrick has dismissed suggestions that Manchester United lacked passion or motivation in their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull City, calling it “lazy” to reduce the performance to a lack of effort.United began their 2026-27 Premier League campaign with a 2-0 defeat at the MKM Stadium despite having 71.7% possession, with Hull scoring twice from set pieces in the first half. The result has led to criticism of United's attitude and desire, but Carrick insists there was more to the defeat than simply a failure to try.United were accused of lacking passion and intensity during the defeat, but Carrick defended his players ahead of Sunday's home meeting with another newly promoted side, Ipswich Town.“Teams lose games and win games, and it's not just because you try or you don't try,” Carrick told a news conference.“There are all sorts of different reasons. Teams lose games, so there's different reasons. I don't have to give you the total reason, because we know what we're trying to improve on.“I think it's so easy and lazy to just say 'team loses a game, everything's wrong.' This is wrong, this is wrong, not trying enough, not enough passion.”Carrick's comments come after a difficult start in which United dominated possession but struggled to turn that control into enough attacking threat, while two first-half set-piece goals left them chasing the game.United now have the chance to respond immediately when Ipswich visit Old Trafford on Sunday for the club's first home match of the season.Carrick lost only two Premier League games last season, against Leeds United and Newcastle United, and United responded with victories on both occasions. The club went on to finish third in the Premier League in 2025-26, with 20 wins, 11 draws and seven defeats.For Carrick, how his players respond to the Hull setback will say more about them than the defeat itself.“I think success comes from how well you deal with setbacks in the end,” Carrick added.“In any position, certainly any sport, particularly this one, going through a season, there's going to be setbacks, sometimes a bit smaller than others.“I think it ultimately decides what type of team you're going to become. So far, we've dealt with those setbacks really well, within games, game to game.“We had one last week. No getting away from it and it's disappointing. But we look to bounce back. We had a good week, boys are refocused, learned from where we could have improved, and keep pushing forward.”
Article Summary: Michael Carrick has dismissed suggestions that Manchester United lacked passion or motivation in their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull City. United began their 2026-27 Premier League campaign with a 2-0 defeat at the MKM Stadium. The result has led to criticism of United's attitude and desire, but Carrick insists there was more to the defeat than simply a failure to try.

Article Title: 'That's a joke': Nasser Hussain slams umpires' decision to abandon England vs Pakistan Day 3 at Lord's
Article Text:
Rain at Lord's

England in control as debate continues

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The decision to end play early on the third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s has sparked criticism after the weather improved soon after the umpires called it off.Rain had disrupted most of Saturday, with the morning session completely washed out and only 24.5 overs possible. Players left the field at 17:08 BST, when conditions still looked poor. But the rain soon stopped, the sky became brighter and ground staff began removing some of the covers.Despite this, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned the day at 18:30, with around an hour of scheduled play still available. Some fans booed the decision, while former England captain Nasser Hussain strongly criticised it."That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports."I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is."In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."The weather stayed dry until the scheduled close at 19:30. Because fewer than 30 overs were played, spectators will receive a 50% ticket refund.England finished the day on 177-7, holding a 357-run lead and looking well placed to win the match and series. Dan Lawrence, unbeaten on 50, said returning for only 40 minutes would not have been ideal."It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50."It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward."Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."The controversy came alongside a similar situation in the County Championship, where Durham were unable to chase four runs against Gloucestershire because of bad light.
Article Summary: England finish day on 177-7, holding a 357-run lead over Pakistan. Players left the field at 17:08 BST, when conditions still looked poor. But the rain soon stopped, the sky became brighter and ground staff began removing some of the covers. Some fans booed the decision, while former England captain Nasser Hussain strongly criticised it.

With the scores tied at 3-3, the match went into a penalty shootout and Belgium came out triumphant 4-3 as India’s men’s team finished a disappointing eighth in the FIH World Cup.Seasoned campaigner Vincent Vanasch showcased why he is considered among the best goalkeepers in the world. Kolkata: India’s best World Cup finish in 52 years has given the women’s hockey team a significant boost in confidence, but coach Sjoerd Marijne believes the real challenge is to sustain that level. In an exclusive conversation with TOI, the Dutchman reflected on India’s campaign, the team’s growing discipline and belief, and the challenges ahead at the Asian Games. Excerpts...I think the discipline, the structure, the talent, the belief and working as a unit made the difference.From the beginning until now, I have seen them enjoying themselves more. They are having fun with each other, they are bonding and they understand the culture and what we want to achieve.The most important thing is that we believe more in ourselves and we have proven that we can achieve at a high level. It’s not just about saying we can do it, we actually did it.We did really well in the tournament, but it doesn’t say anything about the future. The fact that we now beat Germany doesn’t mean we are always going to beat them. The girls have seen that we can do it. I don’t have to tell them anymore because we have proven we can do it. But now we have to do it over and over.I know the expectations are higher now. After the World Cup, everybody now expects more and so do the girls themselves. That’s fine. But we also have to learn to deal with that and we have to focus on ourselves.
Article Summary: India's best World Cup finish in 52 years has given the women’s hockey team a significant boost in confidence. Coach Sjoerd Marijne believes the real challenge is to sustain that level. High expectations, pressure to perform and adapting to new strategies are the biggest challenges ahead at the Asian Games.

Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday, reflecting on his career, family and the people who helped him along the way.The 45-year-old Swiss great, who won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, was inducted alongside former player and broadcaster Mary Carillo.Federer was introduced by his wife, Mirka, and admitted that following her speech would be difficult.“Oh man,” were the first words from the first man ever to win 20 Grand Slam singles titles. “This is very high level and a tough act to follow.”He later joked: “I don't know if you have been practicing secretly” before praising Mirka.During his nearly 30-minute speech, Federer became emotional while remembering childhood hero Stefan Edberg, longtime coach Severin Luthi and, most importantly, Mirka.Watch:“Now the Mirka part,” he said, pausing before breaking into tears. “Oh gosh, this such a mess.”As he tried to regain his composure, Federer told the audience, “I need tissues and sunglasses, everything to protect me right now.”Federer finished his speech by thanking the ball boys and encouraging future players to continue pushing tennis forward.His remarkable career included eight Wimbledon titles, six Australian Opens and one French Open, making him one of only eight men to complete a career Grand Slam.“I'm thrilled to have made the journey here,” he said. “It's amazing to see yourself in a place like this. To immerse yourself in the history of the sport means a lot to me.”Carillo, inducted as a contributor, was also deeply moved by the honour.King said: “She has earned her spot in sports journalism and she has earned her spot in Newport.”Carillo added: “To walk through these gates here in the company of you people, that was beyond my dreams.”
Article Summary: Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday. The 45-year-old Swiss great, who won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, was inducted alongside former player and broadcaster Mary Carillo. He admitted that following her speech would be difficult.

Article Title: Carlos Alcaraz returns to US Open after four-month injury layoff with tennis world watching
Article Text:
Carlos Alcaraz, of Spain (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New York City: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, like the swirling seasons, has changed.Alexander Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at 29 during a fortnight when temperatures soared at Roland Garros, while world No. 1 Jannik Sinner defended his Wimbledon title. Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar shot up the ATP rankings, climbing from outside the top 500 to the brink of the world’s top 10 in less than a year.It is into this unpredictable landscape that a new-look Alcaraz walks in. The 23-year-old, however, will take comfort from the fact that he returns to competitive tennis at the US Open, the Grand Slam where it all began for him.It was at this sprawling venue in New York’s Queens borough in 2022 that he claimed his maiden major crown and climbed to No. 1 in the rankings for the first time. It was here that he returned to the pinnacle again last year, defeating Sinner to claim his second US Open title.On Monday, Alcaraz, whose long, flowy locks, held back by a thin black headband, have already attracted plenty of wows from the fandom, opens against Roman Safiullin, the 29-year-old who lit up Wimbledon with his fight last month.The Russian also defeated Alcaraz in straight sets at the Paris Masters three years ago.The two most recent Masters 1000 champions, Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are potential quarterfinal opponents for second-seeded Alcaraz, who has 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic in his half.“I’m feeling great,” Alcaraz told international media at his pre-championship conference. “I think that right now it’s (injury) all in my head. I gotta trust my team, I gotta trust my people that tell me it’s gonna be fine. So I just have to go 100%, and stay away from that fear.”“My team and I believe that I’m ready,” he added. “It wasn’t an easy decision. I did whatever it took to be ready. I tried to do everything perfect on and off the court, really long practices, intense practices, just to see how my wrist is going to react.”Alcaraz practised with the 23-year-old Holger Rune, the big-hitting former No. 4, in Murcia before arriving in New York.Even though Alcaraz enters the US Open after a four-month injury break and without a prior hard-court singles match, the second seed is hardly short of expectations. If anything, the last few months have underlined just how much Alcaraz, Sinner and the 39-year-old Djokovic matter to the men’s game.They are the sport’s biggest stars, the ones who put bums on seats. At Roland Garros in May-June, with Alcaraz out of tournament play and Sinner’s challenge wilting in the heat, Zverev’s title run became an uncomfortable one for the sport. The German’s two separate sets of domestic abuse allegations reshaped the way he has been covered in parts of the media.Now, with Sinner out with a dodgy right knee, the onus to carry the load for his generation falls on Alcaraz.Daniil Medvedev, the 30-year-old world No. 8, argued that if Alcaraz is at Flushing Meadows, it means he and his team are confident that the wrist has sufficiently recovered.“I don’t think the wrist is going to be a problem,” he said. “It’s more for the whole body itself. If he has a tough match, it could be interesting to see how he copes. It’s really nice for me to see him here to play. If I have a chance, I’m going to watch his match, he’s playing my friend Roman.”
Article Summary: Carlos Alcaraz returns to competitive tennis at the US Open. The 23-year-old injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April. It was at this venue in New York’s Queens borough that he claimed his maiden major crown.

Article Title: Pat Cummins joins the rallying cry for Imran Khan
Article Text:
Pat Cummins and Imran Khan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

LONDON: The deteriorating health of imprisoned former Pakistan cricket captain Imran Khan continues to cause great alarm among the international cricketing fraternity. Expressing deep concern over his condition, cricketers demanded that he gets private medical treatment, is seen by his own doctors and is allowed family visits.On Friday, Pat Cummins became perhaps the first active cricketer to voice his support for Imran's medical care. "I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves," the Australia's Test and ODI captain posted on X."I hope the court ordered medical assessment be allowed to run its course, and that family visits continue," he said, quoting a short clip of former Australian cricketer Greg Chappell on his podcast."Adding my support here to GC (Greg Chappell) and the other former international captains. I hope the court ordered medical assessment to be allowed to run its course, and that family visits continue," Cummins' plea added.Speaking on the Grade Cricketer podcast, Chappell earlier said, "He has been in isolation for three years. I don't think he is allowed books to read. He is in the dark most of the time. Nobody should be kept in those conditions."I know there has been a tradition in Pakistan to have former prime ministers land up in jail, but this is over and above."Whilst no Pakistan cricketers signed Sunday's letter, Javed Miandad, former Pakistan captain and Imran's former teammate, is reportedly trying to visit him in jail. Imran's plight found centrestage during the ongoing Lord's Test between England and Pakistan, when his sons Sulaiman and Kasim, gave an interview to former England captain Michael Atherton during lunch on Thursday.Broadcast by Sky Sports, it prompted a formal complaint from the Pakistan Cricket Board. In Pakistan, PTV, which is broadcasting the series, did not show the 18-minute interview.Kasim told Atherton, "It's very clear what they are doing -- they are blatantly trying to kill him in there." "They just want to keep him in there as long as possible and hopefully just silence him," said Kasim.(With inputs from agencies)
Article Summary: Pat Cummins is the first active cricketer to voice his support for Imran Khan's medical care. "I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves," the Australia's Test and ODI captain posted on X. Imran's plight found centrestage during the ongoing Lord's Test between England and Pakistan.

Article Title: Grand Chess Tour: ‘Praggnanandhaa refused to settle for second place’
Article Text:
Indian Grandmaster Praggnanandhaa

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

CHENNAI: It was the middle of the night in India when golden boy R Praggnanandhaa made history in St Louis, USA. As the 21-year-old became the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour (GCT), his long-time coach RB Ramesh and second, GM Vaibhav Suri, were wide awake back home.For the two men, sleep had been the last thing on their minds over the past month as they kept a close watch on Pragg’s campaign in St Louis. After his sensational triumph, Pragg was quick to acknowledge the hours they had put in behind the scenes.“A special appreciation to my trainers, Ramesh sir and Vaibhav. Especially Vaibhav, he compromised his sleep schedule for me. Back home, he was chatting with me despite the time difference. Huge credit to him. He was online throughout… it’s like 3 or 4 am back home,” Pragg said after scripting a remarkable comeback.Pragg overturned a six-point deficit on the final day to beat Fabiano Caruana 15-13. He had been in difficult positions several times during the tournament, but Suri felt it was Pragg’s relentless drive and refusal to give up that helped him rise above them — and, in turn, made the trainer’s job easier.“Six points against a player like Fabiano is not the ideal situation to be in. But the best thing about Pragg is that he has a very strong character. It’s very easy to feel, in a situation like that, when you have very slim chances, ‘Maybe it’s not my tournament’, ‘It’s not my day’, ‘I can let this go.’ He did not feel any of that at all.“I could sense it from the way we were communicating, discussing game strategy, match strategy and opening prep. It’s much easier for me and the others around him to put in that effort when you know the person you’re helping is extremely driven and really wants this. Obviously, at this stage, you don’t want to be satisfied with second place or simply being a GCT finalist,” Suri, beaming with pride, told TOI from New Delhi.That mindset has been central to Pragg’s evolution as a player. No longer the precocious kid who announced himself on the world stage, he has grown into a more complete player — one who can hold his own across all three formats. His results this year have been telling.After a disappointing outing at the Candidates in April, Pragg won Norway Chess, followed it up with the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz title, finished runner-up at the Sinquefield Cup and now has the GCT crown.Ramesh, who has guided Pragg since he was a wide-eyed child, feels his protege is now playing with greater confidence, particularly in shorter time controls, which have not always been his strongest suit.“Winning such big events always gives tremendous confidence,” Ramesh told TOI. “I think that is very important. Being consistent across all three formats is not easy. If they do well in one format, they struggle in another. But he has done well in all three. I hope this is just the beginning because he has to do this consistently across all four formats. That won’t be easy because adapting to different time controls is not easy. ”
Article Summary: R Praggnanandhaa is the first Indian to win the Grand Chess Tour. The 21-year- old overturned a six-point deficit on the final day to beat Fabiano Caruana 15-13. His long-time coach RB Ramesh and second, GM Vaibhav Suri, were wide awake back home.

Article Title: ‘CoE cannot be only for contracted players’: VVS Laxman on building India’s cricket pipeline
Article Text:

From a compact facility at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium to the expansive centre, how has the journey been?

What, according to you, has been the biggest change?

While contracted players benefit from the facility, how has it been working with domestic players, giving them more access to technology, quality coaching, and support staff?

VVS Laxman with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

There has been a lot of focus on camps in the North East; can you elaborate?

How do they get more exposure?

How has the introduction of the U-15 category for women helped in identifying players?

When you switch roles from administrator to mentor coach, does it help that you see these players up close as an administrator?

When you look back at the almost five years of your journey at NCA/CoE, what’s the most satisfying aspect?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in December 2021. What began at a modest facility inside the M Chinnaswamy Stadium has since evolved into a much larger assignment, with Laxman now at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence, the state-of-the-art facility on the outskirts of the city.The Hyderabadi, whose playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience, is set to complete his tenure later this year.In an exclusive interview with TOI, Laxman reflects on his journey at the CoE, the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition, evolve and transform.ExcerptsIt has been a very fulfilling journey. When I started in late December 2021, we were working with a relatively small facility, and today we have a much larger and more comprehensive Centre of Excellence. The then BCCI secretary and current ICC chairman, Jay Shah, deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to invest in this facility and create an ecosystem of this scale. I am also grateful to the leadership for giving me the freedom and trust to develop and execute the vision we had for the CoE.For me, the biggest change is not just the infrastructure but also the ecosystem we have built around it, bringing together coaching, sports science, technology and education.This is extremely important to the BCCI. The CoE cannot be only for contracted players. If we want to strengthen Indian cricket, we have to strengthen the pathway beneath the international level as well.We are therefore trying to give domestic and pathway players greater access to quality coaching, sports science, performance analysis and technology. The idea is to identify potential early and give players the right environment to develop. Ultimately, CoE should contribute to the entire Indian cricket ecosystem, not just one particular group of players.It is a very encouraging trend. Players who have played at the first-class or international level have enormous knowledge and experience, and naturally many of them want to give something back to the game. But playing and coaching are two different skill sets. That is why coach education is important. We help them understand communication, planning, leadership and most importantly, how to transfer their experience to another player. More players are now recognising that their impact on the game can continue well beyond their playing careers.It’s not one session; it’s an ongoing mentoring process. Transition from player to coach doesn’t happen overnight. It is really a change in mindset. As a player, your primary responsibility is your own performance. As a coach, your responsibility is to make other people better. Through our coaching courses, we expose former and current players to communication, leadership, planning, managing different personalities and understanding individual players. The biggest learning is that coaching is not about showing people how much you know, but it is about helping the player discover how much they can achieve.The scale of our high performance work has grown significantly. Throughout the year, we run programmes across the pathway for both men and women players from the U-16, U-19, and U-23 age groups, as well as targeted specialist skill camps, including fast and spin bowler camps. We now directly support more than 150 players annually, and the impact is clear in the outcomes we are seeing: improved skill levels, stronger readiness for international cricket, and more players progressing successfully through the pathway into higher levels. Our objective is to create a continuous pathway from age group cricket right through to international level.It has been a very exciting process because women’s cricket in India has grown tremendously. The support ecosystem has to grow at the same pace. We are working on a more structured system around women’s cricket. We are also investing in developing coaches and support staff. Importantly, we don’t want to copy the men’s system. Women’s cricket has its own requirements, and we need to develop expertise around those specific needs.That is one of the most rewarding parts of my role. When you see a young player come into the CoE with potential and then watch him develop not just as a cricketer but also as a person, it gives you enormous satisfaction. With U-19 players, you are dealing with an important stage of their development. You are not just preparing them for the next tournament; you are trying to give them the habits, discipline, resilience, and awareness for a long career. When you subsequently see them progress into India A or senior cricket, it is incredibly satisfying.So with the under-19s or the A-teams, it's about getting better every day as a player in every aspect of their game. So it's not only about skill, but the mental aspect, the physical aspect, and how they can improve, because at the end of the day, any sport you play, any match you play, if you don't have that competitive spirit, then you're not a sports person.So you go out there to perform, you go out there to win the match and win the series, but at the same time, whether it's with under-19s or with the India players, it's also about measuring objectively how you're progressing after every match.It’s satisfying when you see that progress in a player because the whole endeavour is: Can they reach a stage where they can win matches for the senior Indian team in any international fixture and also perform at the highest level?The domestic circuit and structure is so robust, and there are so many matches happening across the different age groups. There's a lot of emphasis on developing the talent in the North-East.So we have camps which are dedicated to the North-East players, men and women from U-19 to senior age group. It’s great to see that every year the quality of those players has definitely gotten better, and the only way it will get better is if they get more exposure.By playing against good teams. You test yourself and gain confidence only when you play against good teams and do well; that's how they get exposure.We started it three years ago. It allows us to strengthen the bench and see players develop. We have players from the first batch who went on to play for India. G Kamalini was in the first batch of the U-15 tournament, and she played for India. So it's great to see not only the boys, but also the girls, benefiting from the various tournaments and camps we run under the BCCI umbrella.Coaching and mentoring come naturally because, as an India player, my interactions with the youngsters were always very seamless and holistic. You share your experiences, help them evolve and develop as cricketers, and maximise their potential.The administration part is obviously a different experience, and luckily again, the structures in the BCCI system made that seamless as well. The best part of this role is getting to see so many players come, perform, get selected, attend the camps, and repeat the process the next year.So it's great to see some of the players who were attending the U-19 camps in 2022 playing for India in 2025-26.The most satisfying thing has been seeing the ecosystem come together. It is not about one facility or one individual. It is about coaches, SSM professionals, performance analysts, grounds staff, administrators and players all working towards the same objective. I am particularly proud that the CoE has evolved into a place where players don’t come only when they are injured. They come to develop their skills, improve physically, learn and become better cricketers.The most fulfilling part of this journey as the CoE head of cricket has been seeing the players' transformation, and we hope they've now achieved their dream and will continue to bring laurels to the country.Ultimately, the real success will be when these systems continue to benefit Indian cricket for many years to come.
Article Summary: VVS Laxman has been at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence since December 2021. The Hyderabadi is set to complete his tenure later this year. He talks about the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition.

Article Title: 'Off-field stuff, we don’t focus on it': Muzumdar refuses to be drawn into India-Pakistan handshake debate
Article Text:
Harmanpreet Kaur, Amol Muzumdar

Handshake protocol continues

India look to move on from poor T20I form

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar on Saturday refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol ahead of the team's Women's Asia Cup clash against Pakistan on September 5.With India set to face Pakistan again, Muzumdar said the team was focused solely on its opening game against Thailand on Sunday and would address the issue when the two sides meet.“We try to play the best cricket on the ground and off the field stuff, we don't focus on it. We try to play the best cricket that we know on that particular day. We will speak about this when we play that game. But at the moment, we are focusing on tomorrow's game. One game at a time,” Muzumdar said at the pre-match press conference.The no-handshake stance between Indian and Pakistani cricket teams has been in place since the 2025 Men's Asia Cup, following the Pahalgam terror attack in April that year. India avoided handshakes with Pakistan in all three meetings during that tournament, including the final. The stance was subsequently maintained across senior, women's and age-group cricket.The Indian women's team followed the protocol during their Women's ODI World Cup meeting with Pakistan in Colombo in October 2025. It was also observed during the Men's Rising Stars Asia Cup, the Under-19 Asia Cup, the Under-19 World Cup and the Men's T20 World Cup.The stance continued during the Women's T20 World Cup clash between India and Pakistan in Birmingham in June 2026, when Harmanpreet Kaur 's team again did not exchange handshakes with their opponents.Muzumdar also played down India's recent T20I record, with the team having lost nine of their 16 matches this year. The coach acknowledged that there is plenty of room for improvement but backed the young side to develop its aggressive style of cricket.“We don't pay too much attention to the form. You are talking about 16 T20Is in the last six months. But at the same time, we know what scope of improvement this team has got,” he said.“There is a huge scope of improvement. There is a young side. We are trying to play some good cricket, good aggressive cricket,'' he added.India will begin their Women's T20 Asia Cup campaign against Thailand on Sunday before turning their attention to the much-anticipated Pakistan clash on September 5.
Article Summary: India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol. India avoided handshakes with Pakistan in all three meetings during that tournament, including the final.

NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan wicketkeeper-batter Moin Khan has joined the growing chorus of voices expressing concern over the deteriorating health of former Pakistan captain and 1992 World Cup-winning leader Imran Khan, urging the country's authorities to ensure that the 73-year-old receives proper medical treatment in jail.Moin, a key member of Pakistan's World Cup-winning side under Imran, released an emotional video message on Saturday in which he appealed to the government, Adiala jail authorities and fellow cricketers to stand up for the former all-rounder. His intervention came shortly after batting great Javed Miandad also made an impassioned appeal in support of Imran.Imran has been incarcerated at Adiala jail in Rawalpindi since 2023 after being convicted in corruption cases, which he continues to deny. Concerns over his health have intensified in recent months, with reports of medical problems and allegations of inadequate medical care.Moin, who played alongside Imran during Pakistan's celebrated 1992 World Cup campaign, said the former captain's contribution to Pakistan cricket could not be forgotten and urged authorities to fulfil his right to receive medical treatment.“Our captain Imran Khan, as you all know, is currently in Adiala jail, and his condition is quite bad at present.One more time, I will urge the authorities, the government of Pakistan and all those people who run the Adiala jail,” Moin said in his video.“My request is that our captain’s right, as a former prime minister, as a citizen of Pakistan, his right to medical care should be honoured. Whatever he needs, it should be seen to,” he added.Moin then made a direct appeal to fellow cricketers to publicly support Imran.“Besides, I also urge other cricketers to speak up and voice their support for him. Imran Khan’s contribution to Pakistan cricket [is immense] and all of us who played in his era learnt a lot from him. He has given Pakistan cricket a lot,” he said.The plea comes amid increasing concern over Imran's health and follows a similar public appeal from Miandad. Pakistan's Supreme Court recently ordered that Imran be taken to hospital for medical examinations. He was subsequently taken to hospital before being returned to prison.The concerns have also prompted a group of former international captains to call for better medical care for Imran. 22 former captains from countries including India, England, the West Indies and New Zealand wrote to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif seeking adequate healthcare and constitutional safeguards for the former Pakistan captain. The letter followed an earlier appeal by 14 former captains in February.Australia captain Pat Cummins has also publicly backed the former captains' appeal.Australia great Greg Chappell, who played an important role in bringing former cricketers together in support of Imran, recently painted a worrying picture of his condition.“At the moment, he's not getting any better. You know, from a physical point of view, it's hard to get information, but I saw a video clip the other day, I'm assuming, of his latest trip to hospital where he was put into a wheelchair to get him to, from wherever he was, to wherever he was going, and he didn't look well at all. He didn't look robust. He didn't look like he could really... get around very much,” Chappell said.“I mean, 73 years of age, so obviously, you know, he's getting older, but, you know, I met up with him in Pakistan 6 years ago, and he was still a strong, robust older man. That's not the case anymore. His right eye apparently [has developed a disability]… he's struggling. He's been in isolation for 3 years,” he added.The issue has also spilled into the cricketing world. The Pakistan Cricket Board lodged a formal complaint against Sky Sports after an interview with Imran's sons, Suleiman and Kasim Khan, was aired during the lunch break on the first day of the ongoing Test at Lord's.
Article Summary: Moin Khan urges Pakistan authorities to ensure Imran Khan receives proper medical treatment in jail. The former wicketkeeper-batter played alongside Imran during Pakistan's 1992 World Cup-winning side. Imran has been incarcerated at Adiala jail in Rawalpindi since 2023. Concerns over his health have intensified in recent months.

England legend Sir Geoffrey Boycott believes Harry Brook possesses the rare batting ability to reach the heights of Sachin Tendulkar and Brian Lara , but fears the current world No. 1 Test batter is not making the most of his extraordinary talent.Boycott, who played 108 Tests and 36 ODIs for England, has been particularly critical of Brook's approach in Test cricket. While acknowledging his exceptional timing, range of shots and reach, the former England captain believes Brook's decision-making and tendency to approach Test deliveries like a white-ball batter are preventing him from fulfilling his enormous potential.“I've said before and I'll say again, I've seen a lot of players. I haven't seen anybody with the talent he's got for a long time. Enormous talent. The timing, the shot playing, he's tall, big reach, but his thinking is just unbelievable,” Boycott said in the ‘Geoffrey Boycott: An Extraordinary Innings’ podcast.Brook remains ranked the world's No. 1 Test batter, but his recent run has not matched the remarkable standards he has set in the format. He has gone more than a year without a Test century.In the first Test against Pakistan at Headingley, Brook scored 91, before making 15 in the ongoing Test at Lord’s.For Boycott, the issue is not a lack of ability but how Brook chooses to use it. The former opener believes the England batter has the talent to join a very exclusive group of all-time greats if he can improve his thinking and become more selective in Test cricket.“If he wants to carry on playing that way, he'll have a decent career, but he has the ability, if he could think better, to be in the realms of Lara and Tendulkar. And, whoa, that's a bit special. To be up in that stratosphere is huge,” Boycott said.“There ain't many above them, except Bradman, and that's special. But he plays one-day cricket to every ball. He doesn't have a look at the ball, he has to bash the first ball. He'll just keep getting caught at mid-off and mid-on and daft places,” he added.Boycott's criticism centres on what he sees as Brook's inability to make the necessary adjustment between white-ball and Test cricket. Brook is also England's white-ball captain, and Boycott believes the aggressive instincts that have served him in limited-overs cricket can become a liability in the longer format.Boycott also revealed that he had previously been offered an opportunity to speak to Brook about his Test batting, but the conversation never materialised.According to Boycott, Brook's uncle approached him last year and asked whether he would speak to the England batter. Boycott said he was happy to help if Brook wanted his advice, but he did not want to impose himself.“His uncle came to me last year and he said, 'Would you have a word with him?' Well, he asked me what I thought of him. I told him exactly this. He said, 'Really?' I said, 'Yeah.' I said that much ability is rare, special.“He said, 'Would you have a word with him?' I said, 'It's not for me to go to him. He might tell me to, you know, off,' I said. But if he asked me, of course I'd help. Why would I not? I gave him my number and never heard a word,” Boycott said.
Article Summary: Sir Geoffrey Boycott believes Harry Brook has the rare batting ability to reach the heights of Sachin Tendulkar and Brian Lara. The former England captain believes Brook's decision-making and tendency to approach Test deliveries like a white-ball batter are preventing him from fulfilling his enormous potential. Boycott revealed he had previously been offered an opportunity to speak to Brook about his Test batting, but the conversation never materialised.

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
