Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:
India's Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

The Sports Ministry hurdle

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:
India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit (PTI Photo)

Invited, but left waiting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place. The incident came just days after he became India's first Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event.

Article Title: How Harsh fought through pain to script CWG history, now targets Asiad medal
Article Text:
How judoka Harsh overcame pain

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Harsh Singh's right knee still swells. It still hurts. Every time the Indian judoka steps onto the mat, he is reminded of the ACL and meniscus tear that nearly derailed his career. But at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, pain took a back seat as the 23-year-old scripted history by becoming India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist."The pain never really goes away," Singh told TOI in an interview on Thursday. "Sometimes my knee still swells up and feels tight. During the CWG, I felt the pain and the knee occasionally got swollen. After surgery, the joint never became exactly the way it was before. There's always a little discomfort during fights. You have to ignore it and continue. The medal kept me going."The historic triumph came less than a year after Singh tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS) in Aug 2025. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition."I was in rehabilitation for almost a year. The entire coaching team at the IIS, recovery specialists and Spencer sir (Mackay, S&C expert) helped me throughout.They rebuilt my strength step by step. Because of the IIS and their entire team, I was able to come back on the mat, qualify for the CWG and represent India," he said.The comeback demanded another battle off the mat. Months away from competition saw his weight rise to nearly 72kg, forcing him to shed more than 12kg to return to his 60kg category. Gold at a ranking tournament and bronze at the senior National championships sealed his place in India's CWG squad.Despite lingering discomfort, Singh dominated in Glasgow, with only a hard-fought semifinal stretching him before he clinched the historic title."The semifinal (against the Australian Pedro Carlos) was the toughest. In the 60kg category, even a small point can decide the match. We didn't want to concede anything and stayed aggressive," he recalled.With CWG gold secured, Singh has already shifted his attention to next year's Asian Games. Training stints in Japan and South Korea are part of his preparations as he looks to bridge the gap with Asia's best."I want to improve my speed, grip and strength. Japanese and Korean players are very fast, so training there will help," he said.Born into a modest family, with his father working as a daily-wage labourer, Singh once trained without owning a judo uniform. Support from the govt's schemes and a privately funded athletes' training centre changed the course of his career."My life has changed because of this medal. More people have started noticing judo," he said. "But the best compliment came from my family. They told me, 'You have made the entire family proud.' That meant more than anything else."Having conquered injury to create CWG history, Singh's next aim is clear — turning a gritty comeback into an Asian Games podium finish.
Article Summary: Harsh Singh became India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist. The 23-year-old tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition.

Article Title: 'I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan': Arshad Nadeem blames Glasgow cold for CWG poor show
Article Text:
Arshad Nadeem (AFP Photo)

Lausanne Diamond League next

Pakistan’s Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds, saying the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.Nadeem managed 77.41 metres with his second throw after opening with a foul. His third attempt was 75.39m, leaving him outside the top eight.“The weather was extremely cold and I personally felt that it affected my body. As you have seen in many of my previous competitions, my run-up is usually very smooth, but this time it wasn’t… because my body had become stiff due to the cold conditions. My fitness was good and my health was fine, but ultimately whatever Allah wills is what happens,” he told reporters on Wednesday.Despite the result, Nadeem said he remains determined to make a strong comeback and urged fans to continue supporting him.“Please don’t lose heart and don’t stop supporting me either. Whatever I have achieved has only been possible because Allah blessed me with the opportunity to do it. The respect and recognition Pakistan has received around the world have come through years of hard work. I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan,” he added.“God willing, I will prepare with full dedication for the upcoming competitions and once again raise Pakistan’s flag on the international stage.”Nadeem also responded to criticism on social media, saying he understood the disappointment among Pakistani fans.“I have heard many things on social media, but I want everyone to remember that I am Pakistan’s son, and I always will be,” he maintained.Nadeem’s next challenge will be the Lausanne Diamond League in Switzerland on August 21. He will face a strong field that includes India’s Neeraj Chopra , Commonwealth champion Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, Keshorn Walcott, Anderson Peters and Thomas Rohler.Nadeem will hope to regain his form before the Asian Games later this year.
Article Summary: Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds. He said the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.

Article Title: Reality check after Commonwealth Games 2026: India’s boxing renaissance to face ultimate Asian exam
Article Text:
New Delhi, Aug 04 (ANI): Union Minister Kiren Rijiju in a group photograph with Indian boxing contingent (@KirenRijiju X/ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s record-breaking boxing campaign at the Commonwealth Games has generated plenty of optimism, but the celebrations will quickly give way to a far sterner test when attention shifts to the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from Sept 19 to Oct 4. After returning from Glasgow with a historic haul of seven gold and three silver medals, India’s boxers now head into what many within the sport regard as the closest thing to the Olympics.The CWG triumph underlined the country’s growing depth, particularly in women’s boxing. Sakshi Chaudhary (51kg), Preeti Pawar (54kg), Jaismine Lamboria (57kg), Priya Ghanghas (60kg) and Arundhati Choudhary (70kg) struck gold, while Sachin Siwach (60kg) and Ankush Panghal (80kg) topped the podium in the men’s competition. Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain, Jadumani Singh and Narender Berwal added silver medals.The challenge in Aichi-Nagoya, however, will be on an entirely different scale. Unlike the Commonwealth Games, the Asian Games will feature continental powerhouses such as Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, China, Chinese Taipei, Japan and North Korea — nations that have consistently dominated the World Championships and the Olympics.Uzbek stars Mirazizbek Mirzakhalilov and Bobo-Usmon Baturov, along with Kazakhstan’s Kairat Yeraliyev and Ablaikhan Zhussupov, are expected to headline a field packed with world-class talent.India will also be without two of its Commonwealth champions. Jaismine (57kg) and Arundhati (70kg) will miss out because their weight categories do not feature in the Asian Games programme, depriving the country of two genuine medal prospects.“The Asian Games for us is like the Olympics,” Boxing Federation of India president Ajay Singh said. “The best teams in the world today are Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and India, and all three are in Asia. Add a strong Chinese contingent and you understand why it is much tougher. You can’t replicate this (CWG) performance at the Asian Games. But if you win a sizeable number of medals at the Asian Games, you can be hopeful of winning medals at the Olympics too.Women’s head coach Santiago Nieva shared a similar assessment while insisting the team remains on the right path.“We can’t guarantee that we will win gold all the time, but we are on the right track. We know how strong the field will be at the Asian Games. The boxers are aware that they can’t sit on their success,” he said.India had returned with one silver and three bronze medals from the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. The Glasgow CWG showcased the strides the boxing contingent has made. But it’ll be Aichi-Nagoya that is going to reveal whether the progress is enough to challenge Asia’s finest and signal genuine medal potential for the 2028 Olympics.
Article Summary: India's record-breaking boxing campaign at the Commonwealth Games has generated plenty of optimism. But the celebrations will quickly give way to a far sterner test when attention shifts to the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from Sept 19 to Oct 4. India’s boxers now head into what many within the sport regard as the closest thing to the Olympics.

Pakistani boxer Qudratullah has reportedly gone missing in Glasgow, just hours before the country’s Commonwealth Games contingent was scheduled to leave for home.According to a report by Pakistani outlet Geo News, sources in the Pakistan Boxing Federation said Qudratullah was last seen in his hotel room at around 2am. Officials later checked his room and found that he was no longer there.The Pakistan team was due to gather in the hotel lobby at 9am before leaving for Pakistan. However, Qudratullah could not be found when officials checked his room, sources said.His passport and return ticket are reportedly still with the team manager. The incident is not the first such case involving a Pakistani boxer abroad, with another promising boxer, Zohaib, reportedly going missing during an international tour of Italy last year.Pakistan’s 21-member contingent finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with only one medal. Boxer Fatima Zahra won bronze in the women’s 60kg category, giving Pakistan its only podium finish at the Games.The result was Pakistan’s lowest medal tally since the 1998 Commonwealth Games, when the country won one silver. Pakistan had also returned without a medal from the 1990 edition, making Glasgow its poorest CWG campaign in 36 years.Fatima made history by becoming the first Pakistani female boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal and was later chosen to carry the national flag at the closing ceremony.Pakistan’s biggest medal hope, Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem, also failed to finish on the podium after serving as the country’s flagbearer at the opening ceremony.

Article Title: ‘Like preparing for IIT and UPSC together’: Father Murali shares Sreeshankar’s comeback story
Article Text:
Murali Sreeshankar

KOCHI: S Murali gave an unusual analogy to describe the struggles his son, long jumper Sreeshankar Murali, undertook to regain full fitness after a career-threatening knee injury he sustained two years ago.“Sreeshankar’s comeback was as difficult as preparing for the IIT and Civil Services simultaneously,” he told TOI.Murali is currently near Prague, where he is closely monitoring his son’s training ahead of a busy stretch that begins with the World Athletics Continental Tour (silver level) meet in Bhubaneswar on Aug 22, followed by next month’s Asian Games in Japan.“Sreeshankar’s training now revolves around strength and conditioning, along with the prehab and rehab programme designed by coach Wayne Lombard. There is very little time to work on technique. The priority is to protect the knee on his take-off leg,” Murali said.His IIT-UPSC analogy aptly captures the magnitude of the challenge Sreeshankar faced after suffering the devastating injury just months before the 2024 Paris Olympics.Two years later, the journey came full circle when the 27-year-old clinched the silver medal at last week’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.“Of all the medals Sreeshankar has won, this one gives me the greatest satisfaction because of the circumstances under which he achieved it. It reflects his mental toughness and hunger,” Murali said.The conditions in Glasgow were anything but favourable.“It was around 12 degrees Celsius with drizzle and strong winds, making the runway tricky,” Murali said. Despite the difficult conditions, Sreeshankar produced a best jump of 8.09m to finish second.The performance inevitably brought back painful memories of 2024, when the family received a grim diagnosis after Sreeshankar tore the patellar tendon in his take-off leg.“The doctors in Mumbai had not seen an injury like this. I thought he would never be able to walk again,” Murali recalled.“They told us it wasn’t a common sports injury but the kind usually seen after a serious car accident. His knee was completely ruptured.”Determined to find the best treatment, Murali travelled nearly 1,900 miles with his son to Doha’s Aspetar Hospital. “The surgeons reconstructed his knee using four screws.”The Palakkad athlete spent more than eight months away from competition before beginning the long rehabilitation process.The painstaking recovery paid rich dividends. Since returning to elite competition, Sreeshankar has consistently cleared the eight-metre mark, including a season’s best of 8.38m at the Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar in June.“There is no time to bask in the Commonwealth Games glory,” Murali said, pointing to the demanding schedule ahead.Sreeshankar will now turn his attention to the Asian Games in Japan, where he hopes to upgrade the silver medal he won at the previous edition in Hangzhou.“With everything Sreeshankar has gone through, he has every reason to believe he can stand on top of the podium at the Asian Games,” Murali concluded.
Article Summary: Sreeshankar Murali suffered a career-threatening knee injury two years ago. The Palakkad athlete spent more than eight months away from competition before beginning the long rehabilitation process. The 27-year-old clinched the silver medal at last week's Commonwealth Games.

Article Title: ‘For me, there is one’: José Mourinho picks Kylian Mbappé for Ballon d’Or over UCL and World Cup winners
Article Text:
Mourinho picks Mbappé for the Ballon d’Or, insisting individual brilliance should outweigh major trophies/ Image: Real Madrid, AP

Mourinho: Mbappé has already made history

Real Madrid's Bernardo Silva, left, and Kylian Mbappe celebrate after scoring during the La Liga soccer match between Real Madrid and Real Sociedad in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

Mourinho's argument: the Ballon d'Or should not simply follow trophies

Mbappé faces a strong field

Mbappé has never won the Ballon d'Or

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

José Mourinho has thrown his support behind Kylian Mbappé to win the 2026 Ballon d’Or, with the Real Madrid manager arguing that the award should recognise the best individual player in the world rather than simply going to someone who lifted the Champions League or World Cup.Mourinho made the case for his own striker ahead of Real Madrid’s La Liga meeting with Málaga on Sunday, pointing to Mbappé’s remarkable individual year and, in particular, the history he made with France at the World Cup. The comments also put Mbappé ahead of several leading contenders from Paris Saint-Germain and Spain in Mourinho’s assessment of who truly deserves the prize.The Ballon d’Or is generally judged on three broad criteria: individual performance, team achievements, and class and fair play. Individual performance covers a player’s goals, assists, influence and consistency; team achievements consider major club and international trophies, as well as the player’s contribution to them; and class and fair play include sportsmanship, conduct and public image.Mourinho believes Mbappé has a particularly strong claim because of what he achieved individually this summer, even though France did not win the World Cup.“For me, there is one who, individually, made history this summer,” Mourinho said, referring to Mbappé becoming the all-time leading scorer in World Cup history.The France captain finished last season as the top scorer in both La Liga and the Champions League before taking that scoring form onto the international stage. He also scored a hat-trick in Real Madrid's 4-1 victory over Real Sociedad on Wednesday, giving him an immediate boost as the new campaign gets underway.Mbappé's 2025-26 season was already extraordinary before the World Cup. He scored 43 goals in 47 appearances for Real Madrid across all competitions and finished as the leading scorer in both La Liga and the Champions League.His World Cup campaign strengthened his case further, with 10 goals in eight appearances making him the tournament's leading scorer and taking him to the top of the World Cup's all-time scoring charts.Those numbers place Mbappé strongly under the individual-performance criterion, which rewards sustained excellence, attacking output and a player's overall influence throughout the season.Mbappé's biggest problem in the Ballon d'Or race is that, despite his individual numbers, he did not win a major trophy last season, while some of his rivals played starring roles in teams that lifted the biggest prizes.Paris Saint-Germain won the Champions League, while Spain won the World Cup, putting players such as PSG's Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, along with Spain midfielder Rodri, firmly into the conversation.Mourinho, however, does not believe winning those competitions should automatically decide the award.“The best players in the world, there are two, three or four of them, and we know who they are: they’re here,” the Real Madrid manager said, indicating that several of the leading candidates are part of his squad.“You cannot give the Ballon d’Or to a player simply because he won the Champions League or the World Cup,” he added.Mourinho framed the award as something that should recognise players whose individual greatness lasts well beyond the trophies they collect during their careers.“The Ballon d'Or should go to one of those players who, when they retire, we miss them for eternity. Maradona, Cristiano, Messi, R9, Zidane... You can't give the Ballon d'Or to a guy just for winning the UCL or the World Cup.”The Real Madrid manager then took the argument a step further, suggesting that if the award were simply about rewarding the winners of those competitions, then the coaches responsible for those victories would deserve recognition instead.“If we want to reward the Champions League, then give it to Luis Enrique. For the Spanish national team, give it to [Luis] De la Fuente. The best player in the world is something else and he is neither at PSG nor in the Spain team.”Team achievements remain an important part of the award's criteria, but Mourinho's position is that collective success should be weighed alongside a player's personal contribution rather than used as an automatic shortcut to victory.Mbappé is expected to be among the leading names when the 30-player Ballon d'Or shortlist is announced, although he faces competition from several stars who can point to major trophies as part of their cases.Dembélé and Kvaratskhelia have the Champions League title with PSG behind them, while Rodri was part of Spain's World Cup-winning side. England striker Harry Kane is another major contender after his prolific campaign.Mourinho's own squad also gives him several players who could feature prominently in the voting. Vinícius Júnior and Jude Bellingham are both expected to be in contention alongside Mbappé, meaning Real Madrid could have multiple representatives near the top of the rankings.The third criterion, class and fair play, can also influence how a candidate is viewed. It includes a player's behaviour on the pitch, relationship with opponents and officials, conduct away from football and wider public image. Mbappé's leadership as France captain and his standing as one of the sport's most prominent figures will form part of the broader discussion around his candidacy.A victory would also give Mbappé the individual honour that has so far eluded him despite spending years among the world's elite.The Frenchman has consistently featured in Ballon d'Or discussions but has never claimed the prize, and his 2025-26 campaign gave him perhaps his strongest case yet.Now, after finishing as the leading scorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup and becoming the tournament's all-time leading scorer, he enters this year's race with Mourinho publicly arguing that those individual achievements should outweigh the trophies won by his rivals.Real Madrid host Málaga on Sunday as Mourinho's side look for a third consecutive victory to begin their La Liga campaign, with Mbappé arriving into the match fresh from his hat-trick against Real Sociedad and firmly at the centre of the Ballon d'Or conversation.
Article Summary: José Mourinho has backed Kylian Mbappé to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or. The Real Madrid manager believes the award should recognise the best individual player in the world rather than the winner of the Champions League or World Cup. The France captain finished last season as the top scorer in both La Liga and the European Champions League.

Article Title: José Mourinho makes bold Ballon d’Or challenge: ‘Can’t give it to a guy just for winning UCL or World Cup’
Article Text:
Real Madrid's head coach Jose Mourinho sits on the bench before the La Liga soccer match between Real Madrid and Real Sociedad in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

Mourinho wants the award to recognise greatness, not just trophies

Who does Mourinho believe can win it?

With the 2026 Ballon d’Or drawing closer, Jose Mourinho has offered a rather different way of looking at football’s biggest individual prize, arguing that winning the Champions League or World Cup should not automatically put a player at the front of the queue. The Real Madrid manager believes the award should recognise the players who stand out at the very highest level and leave a lasting mark on the sport, rather than simply rewarding whoever happened to collect the biggest trophies.Mourinho made the comments during his press conference ahead of Real Madrid’s LaLiga meeting with newly promoted Malaga, where he also suggested that some of the strongest Ballon d’Or candidates are already playing under him at the Santiago Bernabéu.Mourinho's argument is rooted in the idea that the Ballon d’Or should belong to players whose careers and performances make them impossible to forget, rather than someone whose main case rests on winning a major competition."The Ballon d'Or should go to one of those players who, when they retire, we miss them for eternity. Maradona, Cristiano, Messi, R9, Zidane... You can't give the Ballon d'Or to a guy just for winning the UCL or the World Cup.If you should give it to someone just for winning the UCL, then give it to Luis Enrique."He then made it clear that, in his view, the award should not become a contest based on nationality, club or the biggest trophy won during the season."No, it needs to go to the best player in the world, not necessarily a Spanish guy, or a PSG player. It needs to go to one of the 3-4 best players in the world, and those guys are here. But politics come into the Ballon d'Or, so I don't like getting into politics."Mourinho's comments touch on a long-running debate surrounding the award, where players whose teams win the Champions League, World Cup or other major honours can often gain a significant advantage in the voting, even when another player may have produced a stronger individual season.Although Mourinho did not name a single player as the only deserving candidate in his broader comments, his reference to the "3-4 best players in the world" being at Real Madrid points towards a number of his own stars, including Kylian Mbappé, Vinícius Júnior and Jude Bellingham.Mbappé, in particular, has a compelling case after a remarkable 2025-26 campaign. The French forward scored 43 goals in 47 appearances for Real Madrid across all competitions, while also winning both the LaLiga Golden Boot and the Champions League Golden Boot.His year became even more extraordinary at international level during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Mbappé scored 10 goals in eight appearances, becoming the first player to reach double figures at a World Cup tournament in the 21st century and moving to the top of the competition's all-time scoring charts.That form has continued into the new campaign, with Mbappé recently scoring a hat-trick against Real Sociedad.For a player who has spent much of the past decade being discussed among the world's elite but has never won the Ballon d’Or, the timing could hardly be more interesting.Real Madrid will return to LaLiga action on Sunday, August 30, when they host Málaga CF at the Santiago Bernabéu. Kick-off is scheduled for 8:30 PM IST (5:00 PM local time), with Mourinho and his squad looking to continue their campaign in Spain’s top flight.
Article Summary: Jose Mourinho wants the Ballon d'Or to recognise greatness, not just trophies. The Real Madrid manager believes the award should belong to players who leave a lasting mark on the sport. Mourinho made the comments during his press conference ahead of Real Madrid’s LaLiga meeting with Malaga.

Article Title: Furious Liverpool star loses cool and kicks fourth official’s substitution board after controversial penalty in 2-2 draw
Article Text:
Liverpool's goalkeeper Alisson follows the ball during the English Premier League soccer match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest in Liverpool, England, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Jon Super)

How the penalty controversy unfolded

Liverpool fight back again

Iraola pleased with Munoz's impact

Liverpool still looking to strengthen

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker was left furious after a controversial penalty decision helped Nottingham Forest take the lead at Anfield, and his frustration appeared to boil over after the final whistle as he was reportedly seen kicking the fourth official’s substitution board hard enough to leave a visible hole in it.The incident came during a dramatic 2-2 draw on Saturday, with Liverpool twice forced to fight back after falling behind. The penalty itself became one of the biggest talking points of the match, particularly because of the timing of the decision and the events immediately before it, while Alisson was booked for his furious reaction.Liverpool and Nottingham Forest were level at 1-1 in the 70th minute when the incident unfolded. Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola had been preparing a triple substitution, but fourth official Tim Robinson was not yet ready with the electronic board.That delay gave Forest the opportunity to restart quickly with a throw-in, with the ball reaching former Liverpool player Neco Williams. Williams moved into the box and was brought down by Alisson, prompting referee Sam Barrott to immediately point to the penalty spot.Liverpool's players and bench erupted in protest, with Alisson particularly angry about the decision. The goalkeeper was shown a yellow card for his reaction, while VAR reviewed the incident but did not overturn Barrott's decision.Alisson did make contact with Williams, although reports noted that the contact appeared minimal, and the decision subsequently drew questions from supporters and observers on social media.Forest made Liverpool pay when Morgan Gibbs-White stepped up and converted the penalty, restoring the hosts' deficit and putting Nottingham Forest 2-1 ahead.Liverpool once again found themselves needing a late response, and just as they had done in their opening league fixture against Newcastle United, the Reds found a way back into the game.Florian Wirtz produced the creative spark in the 82nd minute, threading a through-ball towards substitute Victor Munoz, who took his chance brilliantly and fired into the net to make it 2-2.Munoz has now made an immediate impression in both of his Premier League appearances for Liverpool since arriving from Osasuna for a reported €40 million. Against Newcastle, he came off the bench and won a ninth-minute-of-added-time penalty that Dominik Szoboszlai converted for a 2-2 equaliser, and against Forest he came on again before scoring the goal that rescued another point.Wirtz did have a goal ruled out during the match, with the referee's explanation of that decision later shown to Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk on the ref cam.The result means Iraola's Liverpool have now drawn their first two league matches of the campaign against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest, leaving them still searching for their first Premier League victory. Visuals circulating on social media also appeared to show Alisson kicking an fourth official’s substitution board after the final whistle, with the impact leaving a noticeable hole in it.While the result left Liverpool frustrated, Munoz's contribution has given Iraola something positive to take from the opening two games.Speaking after the Forest draw, the Liverpool manager praised the winger's persistence and the defensive work he has contributed alongside his attacking threat."I think Victor has been very good (in) both games... Everything hasn't been perfect, but he's continued trying all the time. He's gone again and again and I like this a lot from the wingers. The other day he contributed with the penalty and today with the goal. I think he has been always a threat. And also, defensively he has helped us a lot, so I'm happy with him, yes."Munoz's back-to-back contributions off the bench could now put him in contention for a starting role as Liverpool look for a way to turn their promising late fight-backs into victories.Iraola is also hoping Liverpool can add another winger before the transfer window closes, with the club reportedly pursuing Ismaïla Sarr and Yankuba Minteh after bids for both players were rejected.The Reds are also close to completing the signing of Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain, with the winger expected to undergo his medical on Sunday and potentially be available for the trip to Ipswich Town on Friday, September 4.Asked about Liverpool's search for another winger earlier this week, Iraola said:"We are trying to sign in that position. We cannot talk about players who are not ours."It is no secret that we are trying to improve to fill those positions because we don't have the numbers. I hope we can have good news but we are not there yet."I don’t know what’s going to happen. We have to patient. I will be comfortable on September 2. Right now, we don’t know. I have in my head what I want, we spoke since the beginning what we want. It’s a matter of closing the deal."Liverpool's immediate concern, however, is turning those draws into wins, with their next Premier League assignment coming away to newly promoted Ipswich Town on September 4.
Article Summary: Liverpool drew 2-2 with Nottingham Forest in the Premier League on Saturday. Victor Munoz came off the bench to score a late equaliser for the Reds. Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker was left furious after a controversial penalty decision. He was reportedly seen kicking the fourth official's substitution board after the match.

NEW DELHI: Former India captain Sunil Chhetri has admitted he feels “a little jealous” watching the current generation get an opportunity to face footballing giants Brazil and Uruguay, revealing that he never got such a chance during his long international career.India are scheduled to host five-time world champions Brazil on October 3 and Uruguay three days later at Kolkata’s Salt Lake Stadium. The high-profile fixtures will give a young Indian side a rare opportunity to test itself against two of South America's biggest footballing nations.“I feel a little jealous as a spectator. In my 24-26 years as a professional and nearly 20 years with the national team, I never got an opportunity like this,” Chhetri told the All India Football Federation (AIFF).The former striker, who retired from international football last year, urged the current players to stay fit, compete with determination and make the most of the opportunity. Despite being away from the national-team setup, Chhetri said he remained confident in the squad's young talent.“This is their time. There are so many talented youngsters in the team. Everyone gets their opportunity; just like I got mine 20 years ago,” he said.Chhetri also refused to second-guess the coaching staff when asked about selection decisions and the omission of certain players, insisting that the coach was best placed to assess the team's requirements.“The coach has to answer that. I'm just a fan now, watching like everyone else,” he said.The 42-year-old, who recently returned to training, also dismissed any immediate prospect of making a comeback with a touch of humour.“I just trained for 20 minutes. I'm around 42 now, I can barely run properly and I'm struggling,” he joked.The Brazil and Uruguay fixtures come at a difficult time for Indian football, with the side currently ranked 138th in the FIFA rankings and uncertainty surrounding the domestic calendar. Chhetri, however, called for optimism and collective responsibility rather than a blame game.“The Indian football graph, for as many years as I’ve played, has always been like this. We’re probably in a phase where things are not going very well, because of what we’ve done with the national team, what we’ve done in the league, etcetera. But we all have to be hopeful,” he said on the sidelines of the Football Players' Association of India's Indian Football Awards 2026.“At the end of the day, it’s going to be fine. It takes time. Looking at all your faces, we all want things to be fine as soon as possible. It will be. I’m always hopeful. Things might be a little bit 'kharab' (bad), but things are going to be fine.”Chhetri also accepted that players must take responsibility for the team's struggles.“I was also a part of the national team. And why has the ranking gone down? It’s because of the way we have played, the games that we should have won but lost. That is the reason why we are where we are. As players, we take responsibility. I took it when I was there,” he said.
Article Summary: Former India captain Sunil Chhetri admits he feels “a little jealous” watching the current generation get an opportunity to face footballing giants Brazil and Uruguay. Ryan Williams arrived in India as an Australian footballer looking for a new challenge. Three years later, the Bengaluru FC winger has become one of the Indian national team's most vocal advocates, embracing both the club and the country as home.The 32-year-old has experienced near misses with Bengaluru FC, adapting to Indian football, and the responsibility of mentoring younger players while representing India. Despite a six-year trophy drought at the Sree Kanteerava Stadium, he believes the club is closer to success than results suggest.In this conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Williams, who was roped in by JSW Sports recently, speaks about Bengaluru FC's title ambitions, manager Pep Muñoz's philosophy, the OCI debate, national team pride, and why life in Bengaluru has been an enjoyable chapter of his career.Yeah, probably the last three years of my career has been the most, first and foremost, transformative, I would say, definitely. But also the one I've enjoyed the most with kind of what I'm doing with BFC, although we haven't won anything.My everyday life here, I love it. I love living in Bangalore, the football club itself, the way the club is run.Then obviously moving on to the national team has been such an amazing experience for me. It's one that has been so positive and hopefully I can continue to keep it in a positive way and just try and help the younger boys, try and, if possible, get more players like me to do what I've done, for me to show them it is possible. I've said in many interviews that if there is anything I can do, please reach out. And I've had boys reach out, which is good because obviously the reason I'm here is to help Indian football at the end of the day.Not at all. I don't think so at all. I think it's more the fans who have been here to enjoy the super successful times. We have been slowly building and almost got there. The season before I came, they got to three finals. And then the season after, we had a managerial change. Then the season after that, we got to the ISL Cup final. And from our own doing, we couldn't hold out.Obviously last season, with it being a truncated season, just when we kind of found our feet, the season finished. So this season will be really exciting. I don't feel any pressure personally.The fans are amazing. They obviously stick with us through the good and the bad. They're probably the best fans in India in terms of how they do stick behind us when things aren't going so well. So for us, it's more about trying to give them something back. That's how I see it, because they've been so amazing with us, especially with me having come over here from Australia and everything that's come in between.The hardest thing to do as a men's professional footballer is to win trophies. And that's something that, you know, the last three seasons we haven't done since I've been here. So it's definitely something that we've spoken about and something that we want to put right.I'm a pretty well-travelled guy. I moved to the UK by myself when I was 16, moved in with a foster family, had to figure all that out by myself and then back to Australia and then India. So it was difficult the kind of first six to eight weeks in terms of outside of football. But then after that, I kind of found my feet and understood how things worked.And there's still things that I'm not quite 100 percent on, but, you know, I've got a good network of people supporting me, which definitely helped. And then in terms of football, I think any new club you go to, especially a different country as well. I mean, I look back on my first season and towards the end, I started to come through and started to be more confident and got used to the players I'm with, got used to the surroundings, the pitches, even the day to day.I would say one thing that helped me on the pitch was having Simon Grayson (Bengaluru FC manager from 2022 until 23) and his management staff because they were all English and they took the sessions and organised everything the way that I was used to for 12 years in England. So that was a massive help for me. But it did take me the first half of the season to really find my feet and then started to enjoy my football at the end.And then I just kind of kept going, kept believing in myself and got used to (it). Because the European players are obviously different to Indian players and there's positives and negatives about both. So it's trying to work out how do I communicate in a proper way. They all do speak English, that's not the issue. In the UK, you can kind of shout and scream at people and they listen to the message and not how the message is given. Whereas here you have to be more cautious about how you give the message rather than what the message is sometimes. And that's one thing I've been trying to help the young boys with. Just trying to be more positive around them and let them that I'm here to support you. We're both on the same team. We're trying to go for the same thing. So it's in my best interest to help them perform at their maximum capability. In turn, if we win something because of him, everybody wins. So that was one thing that I had to kind of figure out in the first six months.I really like it. I was lucky enough to work with Gerard (Zaragoza) and Sebas (Sebastian Vega) before who have a similar approach... the Spanish management style, which I was new to at first when Gerard came in. So it's put me in good stead because we spent a year and a half or thereabouts together.And last season was good in a way that he [Muñoz] came in. He came in with his coaching staff and it was really good because everybody got to kind of figure out how to work with each other, what exactly he wants to do on the pitch. And that's put us in good stead for this season because last season was, for lack of better words, almost like a draft copy. It was like a dummy run. So now we've been in pre-season early, we're spending a lot more time on the pitch, figuring out exactly what he wants and how we can best do that on the pitch to obviously give us results, put people in positions that works best for everybody. So I'm really excited.I really love what he's doing on the football pitch. And the good thing is that obviously that small part we had with him last season has been, like I said, a dummy run to push us forward into this season. So we don't need as much time together on the grass to connect the dots. The dots are connected and now it's just about fine tuning it and pushing it forward.I think for Indian football, for it to grow at a faster rate than what it is now, we need to see success in the national team. And if that means that the Sports Passport and the OCI can help us in the next one to two years to push us up higher up the rankings and get us qualified for Asian Cups and stuff like that, then there's going to be more interest in Indian football. That's great, but I think long term, I think it would work. I think if we can send the younger boys from here that way, rather than bringing them this way, if that makes sense.If they're looking at just coming here when it [national team] does good, I think maybe they're the wrong kind of people we're looking for. I think we want players that want to come here, give everything for the country and help the national team. And within helping the national team, we actually help the whole ecosystem. So, you know, like for me, there was no guarantees of anything. I have kind of done it because that's what I wanted to do. I'm proud to play for India. There has to be that pride.We want people that wear the jersey with pride and are willing to give everything to play for the country. I think that's what it means to play for your country.There's no city that I've lived in that's like Bengaluru. You know, it is in itself its own kind of country, if you will. Like, first of all, I love the weather. The weather is perfect. If you came straight from the UK, you're in heaven because you have these nice periods where it's nice and cool, like it is now in the rain.And then in the summer, it's nice and warm, but not too hot.You know, the kind of the restaurants here, which my wife and I try to go to as much as possible. There's just so much to do. There's so much to see. There's, you know, so many different aspects to this city that make it beautiful and I really love it all.For me, it's a very relaxed lifestyle. And that's kind of how I like to live my life, in a very relaxed, laidback, not taking things too seriously way. And I feel like here's the perfect place.
Article Summary: Ryan Williams joined ISL club Bengaluru FC in 2023. He has played two games for India so far. The 32-year-old has experienced near misses with the club. Despite a six-year trophy drought, he believes the club is closer to success than results suggest.

Article Title: Double strike from Manisha powers Jharkhand to Subroto Cup U-17 girls' crown
Article Text:
Jharkhand win U-17 girls Subroto Cup 2026

NEW DELHI: Manisha produced the biggest performance of her young career as Jharkhand defeated NCC Aizawl 2-0 to lift the Junior Girls (U-17) title in the 65th Subroto Cup International Football Tournament at the Ambedkar Stadium on Thursday.The forward, wearing jersey No. 12, scored once in each half to settle a fiercely contested final and hand Jharkhand one of the most coveted trophies in Indian school football. Her clinical finishes in the 22nd and 43rd minutes proved enough to separate two evenly matched sides in front of an enthusiastic crowd.The victory capped a memorable campaign for Jharkhand, whose disciplined defending and quick transitions consistently troubled an NCC side that had impressed throughout the tournament. While NCC enjoyed spells of possession, Jharkhand remained composed under pressure and made the most of their chances in the final third.The breakthrough arrived midway through the opening half. After a sustained spell of attacking pressure, Manisha found space inside the box and calmly slotted home to give Jharkhand a deserved lead. The goal injected confidence into the side, with the midfield working tirelessly to deny NCC any rhythm before the interval.NCC responded positively after conceding and attempted to level the contest through attacks from the flanks, but Jharkhand goalkeeper Khushboo Kumari marshaled her defense superbly. Her assured handling and timely interceptions ensured the lead remained intact heading into the break.Jharkhand doubled their advantage just before halftime through the same source. Manisha once again timed her run to perfection and finished with conviction, leaving the goalkeeper with little chance. The second goal shifted the momentum firmly in Jharkhand's favor and gave the eventual champions a comfortable cushion.Despite trailing by two goals, NCC refused to surrender. The runners-up pressed aggressively after the restart and created a handful of promising opportunities, but Jharkhand's backline stood resolute. Khushboo continued to command her penalty area confidently, frustrating every attempt at a comeback as the clock ticked down.When the final whistle blew, jubilant celebrations erupted among the Jharkhand players and coaching staff, who embraced on the pitch after completing a remarkable title-winning run. The triumph also highlighted the growing strength of girls' football in the state, with the team displaying both technical quality and remarkable composure throughout the competition.The final formed the centerpiece of a colorful closing ceremony that celebrated the legacy of the Subroto Cup, now in its 65th edition. The day's festivities began with a spectacular aerial display by the Air Devil Sky Diving Team, followed by an impressive performance from the Air Warrior Drill Team. Students of the Air Force School added a cultural flourish with a vibrant dance presentation before kickoff.The title clash was attended by Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit PVSM AVSM VM VSM, Vice Chief of the Air Staff, who presented the trophies and medals as the chief guest. India women's national team footballer Jyoti Ann Burrett was the guest of honor and congratulated both finalists for showcasing the standard of emerging talent in Indian football.Individual excellence was also recognized during the prize distribution ceremony. Thuamdinpuii of NCC Aizawl was named the best player of the tournament and received a cash award of Rs 50,000 for her outstanding performances. Jharkhand's Khushboo Kumari took home the Best Goalkeeper award, while Beena Kerketta was adjudged the Best Coach after guiding her side to the championship. Mata Rukmanidevi High School of Chhattisgarh won the Best School award, and CISCE was honored with the Fair Play Award, with each recipient receiving Rs 50,000.For Jharkhand, however, the evening belonged to Manisha, whose match-winning brace ensured her team etched its name into Subroto Cup history with a commanding performance on the biggest stage.
Article Summary: Jharkhand win U-17 girls Subroto Cup 2026 with 2-0 win over NCC Aizawl. Manisha scores twice in each half to seal victory. Victory highlights growing strength of girls' football in the state of Chhattisgarh.

Article Title: Chelsea agree to sign Lionel Messi's World Cup winning Argentina teammate in £7.5m deal

Chelsea have agreed a £7.5 million deal to sign Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez ahead of the summer transfer deadline, BBC reported.The 33-year-old Argentina international is set to undergo a medical in London before joining Chelsea's goalkeeping group at Stamford Bridge.The move comes after concerns over the performances of Robert Sanchez, especially during Chelsea's 3-2 win over Fulham on Monday.Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso had identified signing a goalkeeper as a priority after Sanchez's display against Fulham. The deal for Martinez was completed quickly after that decision.Martinez has fallen out of favour at Aston Villa following the club's signing of Japan goalkeeper Zion Suzuki from Parma earlier this month for around £30 million. Martinez is expected to sign a two-year contract with Chelsea, with an option to extend it by another year.Sanchez has been Chelsea's first-choice goalkeeper since 2023. Against Fulham, he allowed Josh King's shot to slip through his hands at the near post. Later in the match, he spilled another effort into a dangerous area, allowing Gonzalo Garcia to score.Chelsea had previously backed Sanchez as their first-choice goalkeeper, but the club has now decided to bring in Martinez just days before the transfer window closes.Chelsea also have Mike Penders, who joined from Genk for £17 million, as another goalkeeping option. He is expected to make his debut in the Carabao Cup against Luton Town on Thursday night.Chelsea are also expected to have a busy end to the transfer window as Manchester City continue their attempts to sign Enzo Fernandez. The Argentina midfielder wants to leave Chelsea and was left out of the squad for Thursday night's Carabao Cup match against Luton.The transfer is another deal between Chelsea and Aston Villa in recent weeks.Chelsea signed Morgan Rogers from Villa for a club-record £117 million, while Alejandro Garnacho moved to Villa on an initial loan deal last month.Chelsea striker Nicolas Jackson was completing a medical at Villa Park on Thursday as he prepares to reunite with his former Villarreal manager Unai Emery. Villa value the deal at around £65 million.The two clubs have completed several transfers recently, including Ian Maatsen joining Villa and Omari Kellyman moving to Chelsea in a deal that was widely described as a PSR swap.Martinez had also attracted interest from Juventus earlier in the transfer window, but that move collapsed because of concerns over a finger injury. Juventus later signed Tottenham goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario on loan.
Article Summary: Chelsea have agreed a £7.5 million deal to sign Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez. The 33-year-old Argentina international is set to undergo a medical in London before joining Chelsea's goalkeeping group. The move comes after concerns over the performances of Robert Sanchez, especially during Chelsea's 3-2 win over Fulham.

Article Title: Career turning point: "Anytime you lose a Super Bowl, it's the worst thing in the world...it will stick with you the rest of your career"- Patrick Mahomes reveals what Chiefs' loss means for his futur
Article Text:
Patrick Mahomes (Image via Getty Images)

Patrick Mahomes spoke after Chiefs' Super Bowl LIX loss

Patrick Mahomes compared Eagles defeat with Super Bowl LV loss

Why the Super Bowl loss mattered so much to Patrick Mahomes

Patrick Mahomes vowed to use the defeat as fuel

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Patrick Mahomes had spent years making the Super Bowl feel almost routine. Then came a night in New Orleans that exposed the other side of that success. After the Kansas City Chiefs were beaten 40-22 by the Philadelphia Eagles in Super Bowl LIX, Mahomes stood in front of reporters and spoke about a pain he knew would not disappear quickly. His message was clear: the defeat would become part of what drives him.Mahomes made the remarks during his postgame press conference at Caesars Superdome on February 9, 2025. The setting could hardly have been more difficult for the Chiefs quarterback.Kansas City had arrived with a chance to make NFL history. A victory would have made the Chiefs the first team to win three straight Super Bowls. Instead, Philadelphia controlled the game and ended Kansas City's bid for a historic three-peat.Mahomes did not try to hide from his role in the collapse.When asked about the Eagles' defense, he gave them credit for the way they played from start to finish. He also accepted responsibility for his own mistakes, particularly the turnovers that helped Philadelphia seize control.“I can’t turn the ball over early in the game when it’s not going our way,” Mahomes said after the loss, acknowledging that he needed to learn from what happened and improve the next time he got the opportunity.That accountability became one of the strongest themes of his postgame comments.The quarterback had thrown three touchdown passes, but his two interceptions and a lost fumble came at damaging moments. Philadelphia turned those mistakes into points, while its defense repeatedly pressured Kansas City's offense.The result was unlike the close Super Bowl finishes that had defined much of Mahomes' career.The question that produced his memorable quote asked Mahomes to compare the Eagles loss with Kansas City's defeat against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four years earlier.His answer captured just how deeply Super Bowl defeats can affect a player who has experienced the highest level of success."Anytime you lose a Super Bowl, it's the worst thing in the world... it will stick with you the rest of your career"Mahomes had good reason to make that comparison. Super Bowl LV had ended with Tampa Bay beating Kansas City 31-9, another painful defeat on the biggest stage.The two losses were different in their details, but they shared one brutal feature. Both left Mahomes and the Chiefs far short of the standard they had set.The quarterback then explained that the defeats could serve a purpose. Rather than allowing the losses to define him, he viewed them as reminders of what it takes to finish the job when another championship opportunity arrives.Mahomes has often spoken about the value of learning from difficult moments. This time, however, the lesson came after one of the most painful nights of his professional career.The defeat carried more weight because of what Kansas City had already accomplished.The Chiefs had become one of the NFL's defining teams under Mahomes and Andy Reid. They had won three Super Bowls in five seasons and reached the championship game five times in six years.That level of success changes expectations. A season that ends without a championship can feel like failure when a team has become accustomed to playing in February.Mahomes understood that better than most.He had already experienced the emotional difference between winning and losing at the highest level. After the Eagles defeat, he acknowledged that the pain of the losses could remain with him longer than the joy of some victories.That sentiment was echoed by Chiefs coach Andy Reid, who said the loss would hurt because of how much work players and coaches invest in reaching the Super Bowl.The defeat also ended a remarkable run of dominance. Kansas City had entered the game seeking a third consecutive championship, a feat no NFL team had accomplished.Instead, the Eagles' defense dismantled the Chiefs' offense and forced Mahomes into one of the toughest games of his career.What made Mahomes' comments notable was not simply the disappointment. It was what he intended to do with it.The quarterback did not describe the loss as something he wanted to forget. He viewed it as a permanent reminder.His message was especially striking because he had already experienced three Super Bowl victories before turning 30. That success has made his standard unusually high, but it has also given him a clear understanding of how rare these opportunities are.Mahomes knows a team cannot assume it will return to the Super Bowl every year. Injuries, competition and small mistakes can end a championship run in an instant.That is why the Eagles loss could become an important chapter in his career.The Chiefs still had a championship-caliber quarterback, a respected coaching staff and a roster capable of competing at the highest level. But the defeat exposed areas that needed attention. Mahomes' turnovers were among them, and he made no attempt to shift blame elsewhere.The response also showed the mindset that has helped define his career. He was disappointed, but he was already looking toward the next opportunity.For Mahomes, the lasting impact of Super Bowl LIX may not be the score or the frustration of watching Philadelphia celebrate. It may be the memory of how the game felt and the lessons he takes from it.That is what gives his words lasting significance.Super Bowl losses can become scars. For Mahomes, they can also become fuel. His challenge now is to make sure the memory of the Eagles' dominant victory pushes him toward a stronger version of himself when Kansas City gets another chance to play for the Lombardi Trophy.
Article Summary: Patrick Mahomes spoke after Chiefs' Super Bowl LIX loss. Chiefs quarterback compared Eagles defeat with Super Bowl LV loss. Mahomes vowed to use the defeat as fuel for the rest of his career. He had already experienced three Super Bowls before turning 30.
